catalog_quote: III. Der Akzent. Der Akzent kommt bei den einsilbigen Worten, die ja in der Wutesprache vorherrschen, nicht in Betracht. Bei mehrsilbigen ruht der Akzent auf der vorletzten Silbe. Nur die konsonantisch auslautenden Worte betonen die letzte. Der Vokal der ersten Silbe wird bei mehrsilbigen stark verkürzt. z. B. muám, litóṅ, wuáb, kukúṅ usw.; nǫjíri „der Große“, nǫyóṅni „der Beter“, nǫémni „der Gläubige“, nongáre „der Arzt“ usw.; tĭláhe „Schuld“, mĭndéke „Erdnuß“, măngúdu „Papagei“, măgándu „Ehre“, nĭbjamhíb „Hausameise“. IV. Der musikalische Ton. Der musikalische Ton ist im Wute nicht so wesentlich wie in andern Sudansprachen und manchen Bantusprachen. Im Wörterverzeichnis sind die besonders wichtigen Wörter gekennzeichnet. B. Formenlehre. I. Das Substantivum. 1. Der Plural wird in der Regel dadurch gebildet, daß man dem Singular ein b anhängt und dabei den Schlußvokal verdoppelt, z. B. yǫ „der Baum“, pl. yǫǫb „Bäume“, be „der Berg“, pl. beeb „Berge“, nū „der Topf“, pl. nūub „Töpfe“, se „das Grab“, pl. sēeb, to „das Ohr“, pl. tōob usf. Der angehängte Vokal ist dann stets unbetont und kurz. Manchmal ist zwischen beiden Vokalen noch ein h hörbar, z. B. ke, pl. keheb „das Blatt“, li, pl. lihib „das Seil“.

new_statements.translation: III. The accent. The accent does not come into consideration for monosyllabic words, which after all predominate in the Wute language. In polysyllabic words the accent rests on the penultimate syllable. Only words ending in a consonant stress the last syllable. In polysyllables the vowel of the first syllable is strongly shortened. E.g. muám, litóń, wuáb, kukún etc.; nojíri 'the great one', nongáre 'the doctor' etc.; tiláhe 'guilt', mindéke 'groundnut', mangúdu 'parrot'. IV. Musical tone. Musical tone is not as essential in Wute as in other Sudanic languages and some Bantu languages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In polysyllabic words the accent falls on the penult, unless the word ends in a consonant, in which case the final (closed) syllable is stressed; monosyllables (the majority of the lexicon) carry no relevant accent. The first-syllable vowel of polysyllables is strongly shortened. Read as a two-syllable window with closed final syllables attracting stress (final if closed, otherwise penult); a fixed: penultimate syllable reading with a consonant-final exception is the alternative.
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant-final polysyllables stress the final syllable (given as the rule's only exception); monosyllables are excluded from the accent statement. Hofmeister adds that 'musical tone' is less essential in Wute than in other Sudanic and some Bantu languages, whereas the modern SIL description (Thwing 1981/2004) shows a three-level tone system with contours and downstep, so this 1918 accent description may be a pre-phonemic impression of tonal/quantity prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms in a missionary sketch's Lautlehre; examples are single words (nouns, deverbal readers nouns). No phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Hofmeister's 'Wute' (also Bute, Ba-Bude in the text) is Vute, vute1244; Glottolog lists this article under vute1244. The description is based on the author's residence at the Basel Mission station Ndumba (Ngila's town, central Vute area between Tibati and the Sanaga) 1911-1915 and his claim to have dealt with all Wute branches; no dialect is singled out. The transcription is pre-phonemic missionary German-style, and the author downplays tone, which modern SIL work (Thwing 1981/2004) shows to be a three-level system with contours and downstep; treat the accent statement as historical and uncorroborated by any modern source.
